def: Initializes a scalar to the value "integer 0 converted to that type" (a pointer gets the null pointer value, which need not be all-zero bits); classes and arrays are handled recursively with padding bits zeroed, for a union only the first named member is handled, and for a reference nothing is done. Objects with static storage duration are always zero-initialized first.

For a class type: overload resolution with `()` and the selected default constructor is called; for an array: each element is default-initialized; for other types (except `std::meta::info`): no initialization is performed. An object with no initializer is default-initialized.

For a class type: if the constructor selected by default-initialization is not user-provided, the object is first zero-initialized, and then in all cases default-initialized; arrays are value-initialized element by element; other types are zero-initialized. Triggered by `()` and empty braces `{}`, among others.

The condition on a type that permits default-initializing a const object: default-initialization would call a user-provided constructor, or every member has a default member initializer or itself satisfies the condition, etc. `const int x;` does not satisfy it.

Initialization of the `=` form, as well as in argument passing, function return, throw, exception handling, and non-designated aggregate member initialization. Explicit constructors and explicit conversion functions are not considered.

Initialization occurring with parenthesized or braced initializers, *new-initializer*s, `static_cast`, and functional type conversions `T(…)`/`T{…}`. Explicit constructors and conversion functions are also candidates.

In [[dcl.init]] ¶15, the type of the object or reference being initialized (with top-level cv removed); the corresponding "source type" is the type of the initializer expression, defined only when the initializer is a single expression.

An object is deemed constructed when its initialization completes, even if it is not of class type or no constructor is called; the destruction order of static objects ([[basic.start.term]]) is based on this.

The declaration that specifies the initialization of a variable (an explicit initializer or default-initialization). Usually it is the definition; the initializing declaration of a non-inline static data member can be its in-class declaration.

An array, or a class with no user-declared or inherited constructors, no private/protected direct non-static data members or direct base classes, and no virtual functions or virtual base classes. Aggregate initialization does not go through constructors; it initializes element by element.

The elements of an array; for a class, its direct base classes (in declaration order) followed by the direct non-static data members that are not members of anonymous unions (in declaration order). Static members and unnamed bit-fields are not elements.

In aggregate initialization, an element initialized by a designator (via its associated element) or by some initializer-clause that appertains to it (or to its subobject); the remaining elements are initialized from their default member initializers or from `{}`.
The aggregate class D itself, or a direct base class of some aggregate base of D (recursively). In the current draft, designators can name members of an aggregate base.

The correspondence between the initializer-clauses in a braced list and the aggregate elements (or subaggregate elements); when a clause does not begin with `{` and cannot be converted to the subaggregate type, the appertainment analysis "drills into" the subaggregate, and this is brace elision.

Omitting the outer braces of subaggregates in aggregate initialization, as in `int a[2][2] = {1, 2, 3, 4};`. It is implemented by the "appertain" rule; there is no brace elision in parenthesized aggregate initialization.
"cv1 T1" is reference-related to "cv2 T2" if T1 is similar to T2 or T1 is a base class of T2. An rvalue reference cannot bind to an lvalue of a reference-related type.

"cv1 T1" is reference-compatible with "cv2 T2" if "pointer to cv2 T2" can be converted to "pointer to cv1 T1" via a standard conversion sequence. It is a prerequisite for a reference to bind directly.

In reference initialization, all cases other than "implicitly convert the initializer to the referenced type and then materialize" ([[dcl.init.ref]] ¶5.4.2). Affects the implicit conversion sequence for reference binding in overload resolution.

When a reference binds to an rvalue or function lvalue ([[dcl.init.ref]] ¶5.3), the initializer expression itself or the result of converting it via a conversion function; if it is a prvalue, it is materialized with the reference's cv-qualification.

Initialization of an object or reference with a *braced-init-list*. Following the order in [[dcl.init.list]] ¶3, it dispatches to aggregate initialization, constructors (initializer-list constructors preferred), single-element initialization, etc., and forbids top-level narrowing.
List-initialization in a direct-initialization context, such as `T x{…}`, `new T{…}`, `T{…}`.
List-initialization in a copy-initialization context, such as `T x = {…}`, `f({…})`, `return {…};`. If overload resolution selects an explicit constructor, the program is ill-formed.
Direct-initialization that is not list-initialization, such as `T x(a);`, `static_cast<T>(e)`.

A constructor whose first parameter is `std::initializer_list<E>` (or a cv reference to it) and whose remaining parameters all have default arguments. In list-initialization from a non-empty list it is preferred over other constructors.

The `const E[N]` array generated by the implementation when constructing a `std::initializer_list<E>`, whose elements are copy-initialized from the list elements; its lifetime rules are the same as for a temporary bound to a reference, and since C++26 it is a potentially non-unique object.

These kinds of implicit conversions: floating → integer, floating demotion, integer → floating, integer narrowing, and pointer/pointer-to-member → `bool` (each with exceptions such as for constant expressions). Ill-formed at the top level of list-initialization.
